title: Cancer in a drop: Liquid biopsy highlights from the World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC) 2025
author: Nadia Ghazali; Ana Ortega-Franco; Diego de Miguel-Perez; Erick F Saldanha; Konstantinos Venetis; Pasquale Pisapia; Surbhi Singhal; Benjamin A Bleiberg; Carolina Reduzzi; Roberto Borea
text:
Abstract
The role of liquid biopsy in oncological care continues to expand, with multiple studies presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2025 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC 2025). This review summarizes recent advances in liquid biopsy for thoracic oncology, encompassing both non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC).
In early detection and screening, proteomic profiling has identified potential biomarkers predictive of future lung cancer risk. The integration of proteomics with clinical and imaging data can improve pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction. In resectable NSCLC, tumour-informed whole-genome sequencing (WGS) assay demonstrated high sensitivity for minimal residual disease (MRD) detection, with MRD clearance following neoadjuvant osimertinib or chemo-immunotherapy associated with favorable outcomes.
In advanced NSCLC, longitudinal liquid biopsy analyses reveal dynamic subclonal evolution driving early treatment resistance. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) clearance following targeted therapy in MET exon 14 skipping and BRAF-mutated tumors was associated with improved clinical outcomes. Emerging biomarkers such as ctDNA tumour fraction and circulating microRNA signatures are promising for radiotherapy stratification and prediction of immunotherapy-related toxicities.
In SCLC, MRD monitoring enables earlier detection of disease progression and supports ctDNA-guided selection of patients for consolidation immunotherapy following chemotherapy. Overall, these advances demonstrate the expanding role of liquid biopsy in improving early detection, guiding treatment, and improving disease monitoring in lung cancer.
Keywords: Lung cancer, Non-small cell lung cancer, Small cell lung cancer, Liquid biopsy, Circulating tumor DNA, Minimal residual disease
1. Introduction
As a genomically and immunologically complex disease, lung cancer has been at the forefront of precision cancer medicine, particularly in the research and clinical application of liquid biopsy (LB). At the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2025 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC 2025), a wide range of studies highlighted liquid biopsy advancements spanning from early detection and screening, minimal residual disease (MRD) assessment in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), to monitoring of treatment response in metastatic disease, resistance identification, and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). This editorial summarizes key abstracts presented at WCLC 2025 across the major domains of liquid biopsy application in thoracic malignancies (Table 1, Fig. 1).

2. Early detection and screening
The Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium reported lung cancer risk patterns among 1.47 million people who never smoked. Incidence was highest in East/Southeast Asia and similar between sexes across regions. Proteomic profiling of blood has suggested that CEACAM5 and CEACAM6 may serve as biomarkers associated with future lung cancer risk, highlighting potential opportunities for proteomics-based early detection [1]. The INTEGRAL-Proteins for Nodules (INTEGRAL-PEN) study, based on pooled data from five low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening programs with a total of 2039 participants (683 patients with cancer, 687 matched controls with benign nodules, and 669 healthy controls), preliminarily demonstrated that integrating proteomics with clinical and image data improved pulmonary nodule risk prediction using machine learning (ML) approaches. In validation, the model showed promising predictive performance with an overall area under the curve (AUC) of 0.87 at one year and 0.80 at five years for predicting malignancy [2]. A prospective study from South Korea found that DNA methylation markers from serum and bronchial washings samples could help distinguish malignant from benign pulmonary nodules detected by chest computed tomography (CT) screening. The two-gene panel from the bronchial washings (PCDHGA12, PRRX1) was superior to the serum panel in diagnosis, with an AUC of 0.785 [3]. Finally, Xia et al. developed a diagnostic module using ML on peripheral blood immune profiles for 1032 participants, which distinguished malignant from benign nodules (AUC 0.952) [4]. Together, these findings suggest liquid biopsy from blood and bronchial washing, combined with ML models, holds promise as diagnostic tools for early lung cancer detection.
3. Minimal residual disease in early-stage and locally advanced NSCLC
In the early-stage setting, multiple abstracts discussed the use of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and MRD testing. As presented by Leighl et al., ultrasensitive MRD detection using a whole genome sequencing (WGS) tumor-informed assay more frequently detected MRD among patients with clinical stage I NSCLC than traditional first-generation assays, which was associated with shortened relapse-free survival (RFS) [5]. Similarly, in a retrospective analysis of 73 patients with stage I-III NSCLC using the Signatera™ Genome assay, Becherano et al. demonstrated that detectable MRD in the two months following surgery was associated with worse recurrence-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 20, p = 0.00061). Patients with detectable MRD who received adjuvant therapy remained recurrence-free, while no additive benefit was observed with adjuvant therapy among those with undetectable MRD [6]. In an early prospective trial of 73 patients with NSCLC, He et al. found that preoperative detectable MRD was associated with solid lesions, non-adenocarcinoma histology, TP53 mutations, and disease recurrence [7]. In NADIM ADJUVANT, a phase III trial of adjuvant chemo-immunotherapy for resected stage IB-IIIA NSCLC, postoperative detectable MRD was associated with worse disease-free survival (DFS) (HR 5.7; 95 % confidence interval [CI]: 1.0–31.2; p = 0.045) among those in the chemo-immunotherapy arm [8]. In the NeoADAURA clinical trial of neoadjuvant osimertinib for NSCLC harboring a classical EGFR mutation, tumor-informed WGS MRD testing was more sensitive than single-gene testing to track baseline plasma ctDNA levels. Neoadjuvant osimertinib led to increased preoperative MRD clearance, which was associated with major pathological response (MPR) [9]. Applying adjuvant osimertinib after complete resection for NSCLC tumors harboring uncommon EGFR mutations, the ADMIN trial reported adjuvant osimertinib was associated with increased MRD clearance (50 %) and improved plasma EGFR mutation clearance (62.5 %) [10]. In the locally advanced setting in the NADIM II trial, elevated histamine and 4-acetamidobutyric acid detected via metabolic profiling of baseline plasma samples were associated with higher rates of pathologic complete response (pCR) and improved survival in the nivolumab arm, but not with chemotherapy alone [11]. While previous studies and those presented at WCLC 2025 demonstrate detectable MRD is associated with worse clinical outcomes, future research is needed to define whether intervening at the time of MRD detection can improve outcomes.
4. Metastatic NSCLC: monitoring, response, and ctDNA dynamics
In the metastatic disease setting, Nicos et al. found that low-pass WGS of longitudinal liquid biopsies identified distinct clonal evolution trajectories linked to pembrolizumab response in NSCLC, including rapid subclonal shifts in short responders versus gradual diversity reduction in long responders [12]. Among patients with NSCLC harboring a MET exon 14 skipping mutation, Xia et al. found that the clearance of the MET exon 14 ctDNA by week 4 of ensartinib treatment was more specific for favorable objective response rates (ORR) and PFS than ctDNA monitoring for other mutations [13]. In advanced BRAF p.V600E NSCLC treated with first-line dabrafenib plus trametinib, higher baseline ctDNA allele frequency correlated with shorter PFS (HR 1.09, p = 0.013) and OS (HR 1.10, p = 0.010), while early ctDNA clearance predicted improved outcomes [14]. Among 29 patients with ORR and evaluable ctDNA enrolled in SHERLOCK, a phase II trial of first-line sotorasib, bevacizumab, and platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC harboring a KRAS p.G12C mutation, 79 % (23/29) had detectable ctDNA at baseline and 95 % (20/21) achieved clearance by week 8 [15]. The dynamics of ctDNA shedding may serve as potential early biomarkers of treatment response and warrants further investigation. Other than blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis can potentially be used to monitor the evolution and response to therapy in patients with brain and leptomeningeal metastasis [16].
5. Resistance detection and biomarker development
Emerging data presented at WCLC 2025 highlight the growing role of LB in resistance monitoring and biomarker-informed management. In the phase II SAVANNAH trial of savolitnib and osimertinib for NSCLC harboring an EGFR mutation and MET amplification, detectable baseline EGFR-mutated ctDNA was associated with worse median PFS (5.7 months) compared to undetectable ctDNA (median PFS 10.4 months). The trial also highlighted an important limitation of LB to detect MET amplification when tissue NGS was used as the gold standard with ctDNA sensitivity 47 % and specificity 86 % [17]. The MARIPOSA study of first-line treatment for NSCLC harboring a classical EGFR mutation showed that amivantamab-lazertinib significantly reduced MET amplification (3.4 % versus 13.1 %, p = 0.002) and secondary EGFR mutations (1.4 % versus 7.6 %, p = 0.01) detected by ctDNA compared with osimertinib [18]. The BRIGHSTAR trial proposed that baseline ctDNA positivity may serve as a prognostic biomarker for response to local consolidative treatment with brigatinib in tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-naïve anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-rearranged metastatic NSCLC [19]. In oligometastatic NSCLC, ctDNA-derived tumor fraction (TF) was a strong independent predictor of outcome after radiotherapy (OS HR = 23.0, PFS HR = 45.2) [20]. Multi-omic CSF analyses in EGFR-mutated brain metastases revealed higher tumor mutation burden (TMB), intratumor heterogeneity (ITH), and immunosuppressive FABP5+ macrophages after TKI resistance [21]. Additionally, liquid biopsy may play a role in predicting adverse events related to specific therapies. Deng et al. highlighted that a circulating three-microRNA (miRNA) signature (miR-193a-5p, miR-378a-3p) could serve as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for checkpoint inhibitor-related pneumonitis in patients [22]. Similarly, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (NGS) in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was proposed to enhance diagnosis of checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis, treatment stratification, and prognosis (p < 0.05) [23]. Together, these studies suggest that ctDNA, CSF, BAL, and serum miRNA-based biomarkers may help detect resistance and inform therapeutic stratification in lung cancer.
6. Small Cell Lung Cancer
The role of liquid biopsy has also been explored in monitoring the efficacy of treatment in SCLC. Three different studies reported results on ctDNA longitudinal monitoring in patients with extensive-stage SCLC receiving first-line chemo-immunotherapy. Yinghui Xu et al. conducted an observational study using longitudinal ctDNA analyses among 13 patients with SCLC and found detectable ctDNA in all patients at baseline, with lower levels correlating with better outcomes. ctDNA decreased during treatment in all patients and rose before radiological progression, with a lead time of two months, demonstrating higher sensitivity for progression detection compared to routine imaging [24]. In another study by Chunxia Su et al., which included 37 patients with longitudinal sampling, baseline maximum somatic allele frequency was significantly associated with durable clinical benefit (≥6 months) and was independently correlated with both PFS and OS. ctDNA analysis also enabled identification of intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms to chemotherapy [25]. Reduction in ctDNA TF has also been used as a surrogate marker of clinical efficacy in a phase II study evaluating BNT327, a bispecific antibody targeting programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A), plus chemotherapy. More than 80 % of patients showed >90 % reduction in ctDNA TF at cycle 3 day 1, consistent with favorable radiographic responses [26]. Lastly, ctDNA was evaluated in patients with limited stage SCLC treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by immunotherapy (serplulimab) or control. Patients with detectable ctDNA after chemotherapy derived significant benefit from consolidation immunotherapy, whereas those with undetectable ctDNA did not. Combining ctDNA status (detectable versus undetectable) with radiographic response (>60 % versus <60 % tumor shrinkage) enabled stratification into three risk groups: the low-risk group had excellent prognosis with minimal benefit from immunotherapy, while the high-risk group derived the greatest benefit [27].
7. Conclusion and future direction
At present, lung cancer patients continue to face challenges, including late detection of early-stage disease, limited tissue availability for biomarker testing, delayed turnaround times for diagnostic assays, a lack of robust predictive biomarkers to guide treatment selection, and inequitable access to comprehensive molecular testing. These limitations collectively delay timely and optimal treatment for lung cancer patients, particularly as diagnostic and therapeutic pathways continue to rely heavily on tissue-based methods, which may not be feasible or accessible for all patients.
Since the first IASLC consensus in 2021 on the use of liquid biopsy in advanced lung cancer, the landscape has evolved substantially [28]. Liquid biopsy offers a rapid and minimally invasive approach to provide molecular information across the disease continuum. Key studies have important early evidence supporting next-generation ultrasensitive ctDNA-based assays for MRD detection and their potential future utility to guide complex decision-making. Perioperative studies have further demonstrated associations between ctDNA kinetics and improved treatment outcomes. In advanced NSCLC, liquid biopsy not only identifies actionable alterations but also uncovers clonal evolution under therapeutic pressure. While SCLC has historically lacked robust biomarkers, recent findings highlight ctDNA as a promising and accessible tool for disease monitoring, prognostication, and treatment stratification. Beyond ctDNA, increasing efforts are directed toward novel biofluids such as CSF and BAL, as well as circulating metabolic profiling.
Taken together, these developments highlight liquid biopsy as an increasingly important tool in cancer care, with growing applications in diagnosis, therapeutic guidance, and longitudinal disease monitoring. Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, including assay harmonization, prospective clinical validation, particularly in the predictive setting, and equitable global access to liquid biopsy technology. Looking for future possible scenarios, the consolidation of evidence through multicenter prospective trials will be essential to strengthen clinical utility and to facilitate the integration of liquid biopsy into standardized diagnostic and therapeutic pathways. With continued progress, liquid biopsy remains promising for improving lung cancer management and outcomes.
